claim: Participants learned to play a novel board game ('four-in-a-row') across six training sessions.
source: Participants learned to play a novel board game ('four-in-a-row') across six training sessions and repeatedly performed a memory test in which they watched and recalled sequences of moves from the game.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the experimental design.

claim: Participants gradually became better at remembering sequences from the game as their schema developed.
source: We found that participants gradually became better at remembering sequences from the game as their schema developed, driven by improved accuracy for schema-consistent moves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Memory improvement was driven by improved accuracy for schema-consistent moves.
source: We found that participants gradually became better at remembering sequences from the game as their schema developed, driven by improved accuracy for schema-consistent moves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Increased predictive eye movements during encoding were associated with better memory.
source: Eye tracking revealed that increased predictive eye movements during encoding, which were most prevalent in expert players, were associated with better memory.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by eye-tracking data.

claim: Predictive eye movements were most prevalent in expert players.
source: Eye tracking revealed that increased predictive eye movements during encoding, which were most prevalent in expert players, were associated with better memory.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by correlation between Elo ratings and prediction coefficients.

claim: Prediction is a mechanism by which schematic knowledge can improve episodic memory.
source: Our results identify prediction as a mechanism by which schematic knowledge can improve episodic memory.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by mediation analysis.

claim: Prediction can be defined as a top-down process in which people generate expectations about what they will experience next, based on their previous experiences and the current context.
source: Prediction can be defined as a top-down process in which people generate expectations about what they will experience next, based on their previous experiences and the current context.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction.

claim: Schemas are adaptable knowledge structures reflecting generalized information abstracted from multiple episodic experiences.
source: A particularly important source of prediction is schemas, which are adaptable knowledge structures reflecting generalized information abstracted from multiple episodic experiences (Ghosh and Gilboa, 2014).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Having a detailed and robust schema yields improvements in memory.
source: Previous research has shown that having a detailed and robust schema yields improvements in memory (Alba and Hasher, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Memory improvement from schemas has been attributed in part to processes during recall since schemas provide cues that can be used to retrieve episodic details that would otherwise be forgotten.
source: This memory improvement has been attributed in part to processes during recall since schemas provide cues that can be used to retrieve episodic details that would otherwise be forgotten (Anderson and Pichert, 1978; Watkins and Gardiner, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Schemas could play a role during memory encoding, by helping people represent information more meaningfully.
source: Additionally, schemas could play a role during memory encoding, by helping people represent information more meaningfully (Bransford and Johnson, 1972; Chase and Simon, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Domain experts automatically engage predictive processes.
source: There is evidence that domain experts (i.e. people with a strong schema in a specific field) automatically engage these predictive processes; for example, basketball experts shown a clip from a game tended to remember the final positions of the players as being ahead of their actual positions (Gorman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on basketball experts.

claim: Basketball experts shown a clip from a game tended to remember the final positions of the players as being ahead of their actual positions.
source: There is evidence that domain experts (i.e. people with a strong schema in a specific field) automatically engage these predictive processes; for example, basketball experts shown a clip from a game tended to remember the final positions of the players as being ahead of their actual positions (Gorman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Predictive processes are only possible with a pre-existing schema.
source: These predictive processes are only possible with a pre-existing schema and might partially explain the large literature showing selective memory improvement for schema-consistent (i.e. predictable) information (Anderson, 1981) and highly unexpected information (i.e. prediction errors, Bonasia et al., 2018; Quent et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the nature of prediction and supported by citations.

claim: There is selective memory improvement for schema-consistent (i.e. predictable) information.
source: These predictive processes are only possible with a pre-existing schema and might partially explain the large literature showing selective memory improvement for schema-consistent (i.e. predictable) information (Anderson, 1981) and highly unexpected information (i.e. prediction errors, Bonasia et al., 2018; Quent et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is selective memory improvement for highly unexpected information (i.e. prediction errors).
source: These predictive processes are only possible with a pre-existing schema and might partially explain the large literature showing selective memory improvement for schema-consistent (i.e. predictable) information (Anderson, 1981) and highly unexpected information (i.e. prediction errors, Bonasia et al., 2018; Quent et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Four-in-a-row is a two-player game where players compete to be the first to connect four pieces in a row on a 4 × 9 board.
source: Specifically, we have participants remember sequences from a simple board game recently developed by van Opheusden et al., 2021 called four-in-a-row. In this two-player game, a generalization of tic-tac-toe, players compete to be the first to connect four pieces in a row on a 4 × 9 board.
evidence: This is a description of the game used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: Four-in-a-row is a generalization of tic-tac-toe.
source: Specifically, we have participants remember sequences from a simple board game recently developed by van Opheusden et al., 2021 called four-in-a-row. In this two-player game, a generalization of tic-tac-toe, players compete to be the first to connect four pieces in a row on a 4 × 9 board.
evidence: This is stated in the description of the game.

claim: Expertise in four-in-a-row has been shown to change how individual game boards are remembered, with experts better representing arrangements of pieces that are strategically important.
source: Expertise in four-in-a-row has been shown to change how individual game boards are remembered, with experts better representing arrangements of pieces that are strategically important (van Opheusden et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Near-optimal play in four-in-a-row can be captured with a linear model.
source: The game has a complexity far exceeding typical tasks in previous schema and prediction research, yet it is possible to capture near-optimal play with a linear model.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the game and is demonstrated by the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Participants start the experiment without a schema for four-in-a-row.
source: The novelty and simplicity of the game ensure that participants start the experiment without a schema but can acquire the schema over several hours of practice, allowing us to tractably study how schema development is related to changes in prediction and memory longitudinally in a lab setting.
evidence: This is stated as a design feature of the experiment.

claim: Participants can acquire the schema for four-in-a-row over several hours of practice.
source: The novelty and simplicity of the game ensure that participants start the experiment without a schema but can acquire the schema over several hours of practice, allowing us to tractably study how schema development is related to changes in prediction and memory longitudinally in a lab setting.
evidence: This is stated as a design feature and supported by the observed improvements in gameplay.

claim: Possible moves in four-in-a-row correspond to different spatial locations, allowing eye movements to be used as an indication of people's predictive processes.
source: The fact that possible moves correspond to different spatial locations allows us to use eye movements as an indication of people's predictive processes, as in previous paradigms with spatial actions (e.g. Tal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage and supported by citation to similar approaches.

claim: Studies of memory for complex memoranda such as chess boards have shown an advantage for schema-consistent stimuli.
source: Although previous research has sometimes found novelty-driven memory improvements for schema-inconsistent information (reviewed in Frank and Kafkas, 2021), studies of memory for complex memoranda such as chess boards have shown an advantage for schema-consistent stimuli (e.g. board positions from actual chess games) (Gobet and Waters, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on chess.

claim: People's schema quality should be related to their memory performance, such that people with stronger gameplay abilities will have better sequence memory.
source: People's schema quality should also be related to their memory performance, such that people with stronger gameplay abilities will have better sequence memory.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: People's eye movements should become more anticipatory as they gain more experience playing the game.
source: If the prediction is indeed a potential mechanism for schema-related improvement, we would expect people's eye movements to become more anticipatory as they gain more experience playing the game and can rely more on internal predictive models.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: The extent of predictive eye movements should mediate the relationship between schema quality and memory performance.
source: The extent of predictive eye movements should also mediate the relationship between schema quality and memory performance, providing a mechanism through which schematic knowledge can impact episodic memory.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: Participants' recall accuracy improved from 61.6% (SD = 18.1%) in session 1 to 69.5% (SD = 20.6%) in session 6.
source: Participants recall accuracy (combined across the online and in-lab data), calculated as the percent of moves they recalled at the right location in the right order, improved across training sessions, improving from 61.6% (SD = 18.1%) in session 1 to 69.5% (SD = 20.6%) in session 6 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Participants' playing strength, measured with an Elo rating, increased across sessions.
source: At the same time, participants' playing strength, measured with an Elo rating (Elo, 1978), increased (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The fixed effect of session was significant in predicting recall accuracy (β=0.015, t=3.215, p=0.003).
source: The fixed effect of the session was significant in both models (for memory, β=0.015, t=3.215, p=0.003; for Elo, β=24.92, t=5.102, p<0.001), demonstrating improvement in both recall accuracy and gameplay over time.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects modeling.

claim: The fixed effect of session was significant in predicting Elo (β=24.92, t=5.102, p<0.001).
source: The fixed effect of the session was significant in both models (for memory, β=0.015, t=3.215, p=0.003; for Elo, β=24.92, t=5.102, p<0.001), demonstrating improvement in both recall accuracy and gameplay over time.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects modeling.

claim: Elo rating in a session was correlated with memory performance in the following session (Pearson r=0.298, p<0.001).
source: We also found that Elo's rating in a session was correlated with memory performance in the following session, Pearson r=0.298, p<0.001 (Figure 2c), showing that having a better schema for the game was associated with better episodic memory for move sequences.
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The relationship between Elo and memory accuracy was not significant within individual participants (β=0.012, t=1.196, p=0.242).
source: We found that the relationship between Elo and memory accuracy was not significant in this model (β=0.012, t=1.196, p=0.242), suggesting that this effect was primarily driven by individual differences (people with better schema tend to have better memory) rather than across-session improvements in Elo.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects modeling with per-participant slopes.

claim: The effect of Elo on memory was primarily driven by individual differences rather than across-session improvements.
source: We found that the relationship between Elo and memory accuracy was not significant in this model (β=0.012, t=1.196, p=0.242), suggesting that this effect was primarily driven by individual differences (people with better schema tend to have better memory) rather than across-session improvements in Elo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: In sessions 2–6, memory for sequences that ended in a win state was significantly better (t=6.67, p<0.001).
source: Indeed, we found that in sessions 2–6, memory for sequences that ended in a win state was significantly better (t=6.67, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: In session 1, memory for winning sequences was marginally worse (t=–2.01, p=0.052).
source: We did not observe this pattern in the first session (before participants were taught the game rules) and actually found a marginally significant effect in the opposite direction, with worse memory for winning sequences (t=–2.01, p=0.052).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was initially no relationship between the probability of a move and the probability that the move will be remembered in session 1 (β=–0.031, z=–1.813, p=0.07).
source: As shown in Figure 3b, there was initially no relationship between the probability of a move and the probability that the move will be remembered in session 1 (β=–0.031, z=–1.813, p=0.07), but in sessions 2 through 6, schema-consistent moves were more likely to be remembered (all p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In sessions 2 through 6, schema-consistent moves were more likely to be remembered (all p<0.001).
source: As shown in Figure 3b, there was initially no relationship between the probability of a move and the probability that the move will be remembered in session 1 (β=–0.031, z=–1.813, p=0.07), but in sessions 2 through 6, schema-consistent moves were more likely to be remembered (all p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was a main effect of session on memory (β=0.164, z=5.763, p<0.001).
source: We found a main effect of session on memory (β=0.164, z=5.763, p<0.001) but no main effect of move probability (β=–0.0046, z=–0.249, p=0.804).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects logistic regression.

claim: There was no main effect of move probability on memory (β=–0.0046, z=–0.249, p=0.804).
source: We found a main effect of session on memory (β=0.164, z=5.763, p<0.001) but no main effect of move probability (β=–0.0046, z=–0.249, p=0.804).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects logistic regression.

claim: There was a significant interaction between move probability and session on memory (β=0.035, z=7.561, p<0.001).
source: However, there was a significant interaction between move probability and session on memory (β=0.035, z=7.561, p<0.001), indicating that participants became better at remembering schema-consistent moves over the time.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects logistic regression.

claim: Participants became better at remembering schema-consistent moves over time.
source: However, there was a significant interaction between move probability and session on memory (β=0.035, z=7.561, p<0.001), indicating that participants became better at remembering schema-consistent moves over the time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction effect.

claim: Reaction time during retrieval was initially not related to the probability of the move (β=–30.5, t=0.975, p=0.329).
source: Similar to accuracy, we found that reaction time during retrieval was initially not related to the probability of the move (β=–30.5, t=0.975, p=0.329) but consistently faster for more schema-consistent moves in sessions 2 through 6 (all p<0.001, Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Reaction time was consistently faster for more schema-consistent moves in sessions 2 through 6 (all p<0.001).
source: Similar to accuracy, we found that reaction time during retrieval was initially not related to the probability of the move (β=–30.5, t=0.975, p=0.329) but consistently faster for more schema-consistent moves in sessions 2 through 6 (all p<0.001, Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3d.

claim: There was a main effect of session on reaction time (β=–156.3, t=–2.39, p=0.017).
source: Running a mixed-effects model as for the accuracy (using linear rather than logistic regression), we found a main effect of session on reaction time (β=–156.3, t=–2.39, p=0.017), such that participants were faster in later training sessions.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects linear regression.

claim: There was no main effect of move probability on reaction time (β=- 46.1, t=−0.440, p=0.660).
source: There was no main effect of move probability (β=- 46.1, t=−0.440, p=0.660) but a significant interaction between move probability and the session on reaction time (β=−71.06, t=–2.593, p=0.010), with faster responses when remembering more schema-consistent moves.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects linear regression.

claim: There was a significant interaction between move probability and session on reaction time (β=−71.06, t=–2.593, p=0.010).
source: There was no main effect of move probability (β=- 46.1, t=−0.440, p=0.660) but a significant interaction between move probability and the session on reaction time (β=−71.06, t=–2.593, p=0.010), with faster responses when remembering more schema-consistent moves.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects linear regression.

claim: The proportion of schema-consistent mistakes increased over the first 4 training sessions.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3e, the proportion of schema-consistent mistakes increased over the first 4 training sessions.
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 3e.

claim: There was a significant effect of session on the proportion of schema-consistent mistakes (β=0.032, t=5.413, p<0.001).
source: We ran a mixed-effects model with a participant random slope, the proportion of schema-consistent mistakes as the outcome variable, and session as a fixed-effect predictor, and found a significant effect of the session (β=0.032, t=5.413, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed-effects modeling.

claim: The relationship between recall accuracy and move probability was significantly weaker at session 5 (t=–3.24, p=0.001).
source: Although an overall increase across sessions was observed in both schema-consistent mistakes and the relationship between recall accuracy and move probability, these effects were significantly weaker at session 5 (for schema-consistent mistakes, t=–2.51, p=0.02; for the relationship between recall accuracy and move probability, t=–3.24, p=0.001), and numerically weaker at session 6 (for schema consistent mistakes, t=–1.70, p=0.099; for the relationship between recall accuracy and move probability, t=–1.93, p=0.053).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Schema-consistent mistakes were significantly weaker at session 5 (t=–2.51, p=0.02).
source: Although an overall increase across sessions was observed in both schema-consistent mistakes and the relationship between recall accuracy and move probability, these effects were significantly weaker at session 5 (for schema-consistent mistakes, t=–2.51, p=0.02; for the relationship between recall accuracy and move probability, t=–3.24, p=0.001), and numerically weaker at session 6 (for schema consistent mistakes, t=–1.70, p=0.099; for the relationship between recall accuracy and move probability, t=–1.93, p=0.053).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Out of over 1000 moves across 6 sessions there were on average 1.0 repeats (SD = 1.67) that participants experienced during gameplay and were later part of a memory sequence.
source: To test this possibility, we examined all the boards that participants saw during gameplay and the moves played on these boards, and found the repetition of exact move sequences to be very rare; out of over 1000 moves across 6 sessions there were on average 1.0 repeats (SD = 1.67) that participants experienced during gameplay and were later part of a memory sequence.
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the overlap between gameplay and memory sequences.

claim: Purely schema-based guessing can only achieve an average accuracy of 13.39% across the six sessions.
source: We simulated this strategy by drawing moves probabilistically from the gameplay (schema) model for each initial board that participants saw during the memory task in each session. We found that purely schema-based guessing can only achieve an average accuracy of 13.39% across the ix sessions (Figure 2a), which is much lower than participants' average recall accuracy of 65.91%.
evidence: This is a result from simulation shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Participants' average recall accuracy was 65.91%.
source: We found that purely schema-based guessing can only achieve an average accuracy of 13.39% across the ix sessions (Figure 2a), which is much lower than participants' average recall accuracy of 65.91%.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the experimental data.

claim: There was a significant fixed effect of session on prediction coefficient (β=0.009, t=4.261, p<0.001).
source: There was a significant fixed effect of session, β=0.009, t=4.261, p<0.001, providing evidence that people's eye movements became more predictive over training (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 5a.

claim: People's eye movements became more predictive over training.
source: There was a significant fixed effect of session, β=0.009, t=4.261, p<0.001, providing evidence that people's eye movements became more predictive over training (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical result shown in Figure 5a.

claim: More sophisticated gameplay (higher Elo) was associated with more prediction in the next memory session (Pearson r=0.33, p=0.002).
source: We found that, on a session-by-session basis, more sophisticated gameplay (higher Elo) was associated with more prediction in the next memory session (Pearson r=0.33, p=0.002), demonstrating that better players predict more during encoding (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Memory sessions in which a player exhibited high levels of predictive eye movements showed better reconstruction accuracy (Pearson r=0.40, p<0.001).
source: Memory sessions in which a player exhibited high levels of predictive eye movements also showed better reconstruction accuracy (Pearson r=0.40, p<0.001), despite there being no explicit demand to generate predictions during encoding (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The total effect of Elo on recall accuracy was significant (β=0.35, t=3.26, p=0.002).
source: The total effect of Elo on recall accuracy was significant (β=0.35, t=3.26, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mediation analysis.

claim: The effect of Elo on the prediction coefficient was significant (β=0.33, t=3.13. p=0.002).
source: The effect of Elo on the prediction coefficient was also significant, (β=0.33, t=3.13. p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mediation analysis.

claim: The bootstrapped indirect effect was 0.10, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.19], p=0.006.
source: The bootstrapped indirect effect was 0.10, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.19], p=0.006, suggesting that improved memory for better players is partially mediated by improved predictions during encoding.
evidence: This is a statistical result from mediation analysis.

claim: Improved memory for better players is partially mediated by improved predictions during encoding.
source: The bootstrapped indirect effect was 0.10, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.19], p=0.006, suggesting that improved memory for better players is partially mediated by improved predictions during encoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation analysis result.

claim: With the inclusion of the prediction coefficient, the impact of Elo on recall accuracy was reduced but remained significant (β=0.24, t=2.26, p=0.03).
source: With the inclusion of the prediction coefficient, the impact of Elo on recall accuracy was reduced but remained significant (β=0.24, t=2.26, p=0.03), indicating that expertise also improves memory accuracy through additional mechanisms (at encoding and/or retrieval).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mediation analysis.

claim: Expertise improves memory accuracy through additional mechanisms beyond prediction (at encoding and/or retrieval).
source: With the inclusion of the prediction coefficient, the impact of Elo on recall accuracy was reduced but remained significant (β=0.24, t=2.26, p=0.03), indicating that expertise also improves memory accuracy through additional mechanisms (at encoding and/or retrieval).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation analysis result.

claim: There was a main effect of log probability of the move on subsequent memory (β=0.083, z=5.882, p<0.001).
source: There was a main effect of log probability of the move (β=0.083, z=5.882, p<0.001), consistent with our session-level results demonstrating a memory benefit for more likely moves.
evidence: This is a statistical result from move-level logistic regression.

claim: There was a significant effect of prediction coefficient on subsequent memory (β=0.508, z=3.187, p=0.001).
source: We also found a significant effect on the prediction coefficient (β=0.508, z=3.187, p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from move-level logistic regression.

claim: There is no interaction between the move probability and prediction coefficient (β=0.024, z=0.395, p=0.693).
source: There is no interaction between the move probability and prediction coefficient (β=0.024, z=0.395, p=0.693).
evidence: This is a statistical result from move-level logistic regression.

claim: Making schema-consistent predictions before a move appears is correlated with better memory for the move, independent of the schema-consistency of the move.
source: This result shows that making schema-consistent predictions before a move appears is correlated with better memory for the move, independent of the schema-consistency of the move.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the move-level regression results.

claim: Making confident predictions before a move is related to better memory for that move (β=0.375, z=4.372, p<0.001).
source: We found the main effects of both factors, indicating that (a) making confident predictions before a move is related to better memory for that move (β=0.375, z=4.372, p<0.001) and (b) unexpected (surprising) moves are more poorly remembered (β=–0.015, z=–2.448, p=0.014).
evidence: This is a statistical result from move-level logistic regression using model-free measures.

claim: Unexpected (surprising) moves are more poorly remembered (β=–0.015, z=–2.448, p=0.014).
source: We found the main effects of both factors, indicating that (a) making confident predictions before a move is related to better memory for that move (β=0.375, z=4.372, p<0.001) and (b) unexpected (surprising) moves are more poorly remembered (β=–0.015, z=–2.448, p=0.014).
evidence: This is a statistical result from move-level logistic regression using model-free measures.

claim: The mean interval between sessions was 2.15 days.
source: The study used a longitudinal design, in which participants completed six sessions over a period of about one to two weeks (Figure 1a). The mean interval between sessions was 2.15 days.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The first set of 19 participants completed the task online on their home computers.
source: The first set of 19 participants (12 female, six male, and two non-binary) completed the task online on their home computers (and were instructed to maximize their browser windows during the task).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: The online study participants had a mean age of 20.95 years (SD = 2.84).
source: The online study participants had a mean age of 20.95 years (SD = 2.84).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the participant sample.

claim: A second set of 16 participants performed an identical task in the lab while eye-tracking data was collected.
source: A second set of 16 participants (nine female, six male, and one declined to answer) performed an identical task in the lab while eye-tracking data was collected.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: The eye-tracking study participants had a mean age of 21.81 years (SD = 3.21).
source: The eye-tracking study participants had a mean age of 21.81 years (SD = 3.21).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the participant sample.

claim: In the first session, most participants did not suspect that the stimuli were from a game or guess the rules of the game (14 out of 19 in the online study, and 13 out of 16 in the in-person study).
source: In a post-task questionnaire, we confirmed that in session 1 most participants did not suspect that the stimuli were from a game or guess the rules of the game (14 out of 19 in the online study, and 13 out of 16 in the in-person study).
evidence: This is a result from a post-task questionnaire.

claim: The sequences of moves were generated using an AI agent from van Opheusden et al., 2021 with a relatively weak Elo rating similar to participants' average playing strengths during their first session.
source: The sequences of moves were generated using an AI agent from van Opheusden et al., 2021 with an relatively weak Elo rating similar to participants' average playing strengths during their first session.
evidence: This is a description of how stimuli were generated.

claim: Of the 30 sequences in each session, 10 sequences (two of each length) ended with one player winning.
source: Of the 30 sequences in each session, 10 sequences (two of each length) ended with one player winning (i.e. the last move created a four-in-a-row).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus design.

claim: During the gameplay sessions, all participants tended to play moves with relatively high probability under the gameplay model (M=0.213, range=0.143–0.297, compared to a random-move baseline of 0.040).
source: We did not find evidence for this possibility in our dataset; during the gameplay sessions, all participants tended to play moves with relatively high probability under the gameplay model (M=0.213, range=0.143–0.297, compared to a random-move baseline of 0.040).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing participants' gameplay moves.

claim: There was a strong correlation between Elo and move probability measure (r=0.40, p<0.001).
source: We also observed a strong correlation between Elo and this move probability measure (r=0.40, p<0.001), showing that stronger players are more aligned with our model.
evidence: This is a statistical result from analyzing gameplay data.

claim: Stronger players are more aligned with the gameplay model.
source: We also observed a strong correlation between Elo and this move probability measure (r=0.40, p<0.001), showing that stronger players are more aligned with our model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation result.

claim: Eye-tracking data was collected during the memory task on each day for the in-lab subset of participants.
source: For the in-lab subset of participants, eye-tracking data was collected during the memory task on each day.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection procedure.

claim: Binocular eye movement was recorded using EyeLink 1000 plus at 1000 Hz recording frequency.
source: We recorded binocular eye movement using EyeLink 1000 plus at 1000 Hz recording frequency.
evidence: This is a description of the eye-tracking equipment and settings.

claim: The observed mediation effect is primarily driven by individual differences rather than within-subject development over time.
source: Together with previous findings, these results suggest that the observed mediation effect is primarily driven by individual differences rather than within-subject development over time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian mixed-effects model results.

claim: Sherman and Turk-Browne, 2020 showed that making predictions does not benefit memory for the upcoming item and impairs the encoding of the current item.
source: In a recent study, Sherman and Turk-Browne, 2020 showed that making predictions does not benefit memory for the upcoming item and impairs the encoding of the current item, which is inconsistent with our findings.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The explicit schematic predictions in the current study that are based on rules and progression toward goal states might rely on a different network such as the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: On the other hand, the explicit schematic predictions in our study that are based on rules and progression toward goal states might rely on a different network such as the medial prefrontal cortex (Bonasia et al., 2018; Robin and Moscovitch, 2017; van Kesteren et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior research on neural mechanisms.

claim: Potts and Shanks, 2014 demonstrated a benefit even for minimal predictions when predictions are based on random guessing and are wrong almost all the time.
source: Potts and Shanks, 2014 demonstrated a benefit even for minimal predictions when predictions are based on random guessing and are wrong almost all the time.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Chess experts' memory advantage was primarily driven by very high accuracy for schema-consistent (legitimate) boards.
source: Expertise effects that partially extend to non-schematic situations have been previously observed; although chess experts' memory advantage was primarily driven by very high accuracy for schema-consistent (legitimate) boards in Gobet and Waters, 2003, experts also exhibited memory for random boards that was better than that of weaker players.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on chess expertise.

claim: Chess experts exhibited memory for random boards that was better than that of weaker players.
source: Expertise effects that partially extend to non-schematic situations have been previously observed; although chess experts' memory advantage was primarily driven by very high accuracy for schema-consistent (legitimate) boards in Gobet and Waters, 2003, experts also exhibited memory for random boards that was better than that of weaker players.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on chess expertise.

claim: Experts may be able to devote fewer attentional resources to schematic moves, freeing up additional resources to handle more unusual moves.
source: One possibility is that experts may be able to devote fewer attentional resources to schematic moves, freeing up additional resources to handle more unusual moves.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism for the observed pattern.

claim: Participants in the study may have developed an effortful strategy to remember schema-inconsistent moves (such as switching to a shape-based encoding for these moves).
source: Participants in our study may have also developed an effortful strategy to remember schema-inconsistent moves (such as switching to a shape-based encoding for these moves), consistent with the longer reaction times observed for low-probability moves in later sessions.
evidence: This is speculation about participant strategies, supported by observed reaction time patterns.

claim: Participants spontaneously exhibited predictive eye movements consistent with the game schema, without any explicit prediction demands.
source: The eye-tracking study showed that participants spontaneously exhibited predictive eye movements consistent with the game schema, without any explicit prediction demands.
evidence: This is a summary of the eye-tracking findings.

claim: Didierjean and Marmèche, 2005 showed automatic predictive representations in basketball experts.
source: This is consistent with earlier work showing automatic predictive representations in basketball experts (Didierjean and Marmèche, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Schema-based predictions were associated with improved memory at the level of participants and the level of individual moves.
source: We also found that schema-based predictions were associated with improved memory (at the level of participants and the level of individual moves) and that these encoding-time predictions provide a mechanism for the impact of schema quality on memory performance.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the eye-tracking analysis.

claim: Encoding-time predictions provide a mechanism for the impact of schema quality on memory performance.
source: We also found that schema-based predictions were associated with improved memory (at the level of participants and the level of individual moves) and that these encoding-time predictions provide a mechanism for the impact of schema quality on memory performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation analysis results.

claim: The biggest increase in prediction occurred between sessions one and two.
source: Second, the biggest increase in prediction occurred between sessions one and two, but the session one memory-task data cannot be included in this prediction model since participants have not yet played the game (and we therefore cannot estimate their Elo).
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of why within-participant effects were not detected.

claim: The session-level analysis provided the novel insight that the memory advantage for more-expert players may be driven by superior predictive processes during encoding.
source: Despite the lack of within-subject effect, the session-level analysis provided the novel insight that the memory advantage for more-expert players may be driven by superior predictive processes during encoding.
evidence: This is stated as a key insight from the analysis.

claim: The implicit learning of arbitrary statistical dependencies between image categories in Sherman and Turk-Browne, 2020 engages a predictive process that relies on the hippocampus.
source: One possibility is that their study (in which participants implicitly learned arbitrary statistical dependencies between image categories presented in a continuous stream) engages a predictive process that relies on the hippocampus (Schapiro et al., 2017), creating interference between prediction and encoding processes.
evidence: This is speculation about neural mechanisms supported by citation.

claim: Four-in-a-row is an exciting testbed for future studies of the cognitive and neural mechanisms of schema development and its impact on episodic memory.
source: This makes four-in-a-row an exciting testbed for future studies of the cognitive and neural mechanisms of schema development and its impact on episodic memory.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the value of the paradigm.
